subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalamu alaikum, and welcome, young scientist! Look around you the next time you walk outside. The bright pink flowers on a hibiscus bush, the sweet-smelling blossoms on a mango tree, the tiny flowers hidden among the tall grass, the yellow tassels waving at the top of a maize plant, the thorny acacia trees that dot the savanna, and even the giant baobab standing like a wise old giant in the dry land are all doing the very same secret job. Every one of these plants is working hard to make new plants. In this unit you will discover exactly how a flower turns into a fruit and how a fruit carries seeds to faraway places. This is one of the most important stories in all of nature, and by the end you will understand it well enough to explain it to your…

Know that insects pollinate some flowers
Observe that plants produce flowers which have male and female organs; seeds are formed when pollen from the male organ fertilises the ovum (female)
Recognise that flowering plants have a life cycle including pollination, fertilisation, seed production, seed dispersal and germination

outcomes: Name and describe the main parts of a flower and explain the job each part does.
Explain pollination and describe how insects such as bees and butterflies, and how the wind, carry pollen from one flower to another.
Describe fertilisation and explain how a flower changes into a fruit after it has been pollinated.
Explain how seeds form inside a fruit and why each seed can grow into a brand-new plant.
Compare the flowers of insect-pollinated plants (like mango) with wind-pollinated plants (like maize).
Describe several ways seeds are dispersed by wind, by water, by animals, and by exploding pods, and explain why spreading out helps plants survive.
Put the whole life cycle in order, from seed to seedling to flowering plant to fruit and back to seed.
Investigate flowers and seeds safely at home and record what you observe like a real scientist.

Scientists use special words so that everyone understands exactly the same thing. Study this table carefully. You do not need to memorise every word today, but come back to it often. Each word is a tool that helps you think clearly.
The reproductive part of a plant that makes seeds.

concepts.title: A Flower Is a Plant's Baby-Making Factory
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin with the flower itself. It is easy to think that flowers exist only to look pretty or to smell nice, but that is not their real purpose. A flower is the part of a plant that makes seeds, and seeds are how plants make new plants. In other words, a flower is a tiny, beautiful factory built for one job: reproduction. Everything about a flower, its colour, its scent, its shape, and its sweet nectar, is a clever tool to help it do that job well.

Imagine you are holding a fresh hibiscus flower, the kind that grows in many gardens along the coast from Mombasa to Lamu. If you look from the outside inward, you will meet the flower's parts one at a time. On the very outside are the sepals. These are the small green parts that once wrapped tightly around the bud like a protective blanket, keeping the delicate flower safe before it opened. Think of the sepals as the guards standing at the door before the flower is ready to greet the world.

Just inside the sepals are the petals. In a hibiscus these are large and bright red, and they are the part everyone notices first. Petals are like a colourful signboard and a welcome mat rolled into one. Their bright colours and sweet smell shout to passing bees, butterflies and birds, "Come here! There is sweet food inside!" The petals are not just decoration; they are an advertisement, and the customers they want to attract are pollinators.

Now we reach the working heart of the flower. Inside the ring of petals stand the stamens, which are the male parts. Each stamen has two pieces: a thin stalk called the filament, and a little bag at the top called the anther. The anther is where pollen is made. Pollen is a fine, often yellow powder, and each tiny grain carries a male cell. If you have ever brushed against a lily and found yellow dust on your sleeve, you have already met pollen. In a hibiscus, the stamens are joined together into a long tube that sticks out proudly from the middle of the flower.

In the very centre is the pistil, which is the female part (some scientists call it the carpel). The pistil has three sections. At the top is the stigma, which is sticky on purpose so that it can catch pollen grains that land on it. Below the stigma is a stalk called the style. At the bottom, hidden and protected, is the ovary. Inside the ovary are tiny ovules, and each ovule is a future seed waiting to be started. Keep that ovary in mind, because later in this unit it is going to grow into something you love to eat.

Here is a helpful way to picture it. If a flower were a house, the sepals would be the fence around the garden, the petals would be the bright front door that invites guests, the stamens would be the bakers making a delicious powder, and the pistil would be the kitchen deep inside where the seeds are actually cooked up. Every part has a job, and the jobs work together.

Did You Know? A single sunflower is not really one flower at all. What looks like one big flower is actually hundreds of tiny flowers packed together, and each little flower can make one seed. That is why one sunflower head can give you so many seeds to roast and eat!
concepts.example: Not all flowers keep their male and female parts in the same blossom. Some plants, such as the maize (corn) that grows in many East African fields, have separate male flowers and female flowers on the same plant. The male flowers form the feathery tassel at the very top, while the female flowers become the cob lower down, each strand of maize silk leading to one future kernel. A flower that carries both male and female parts is sometimes called a perfect flower, and one with only one kind is called an imperfect flower. Both kinds can make seeds, just in slightly different ways.

concepts.title: Pollination, the Great Pollen Journey
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know the parts of a flower, we can watch the first big step of making a seed. That step is called pollination. Pollination simply means moving pollen from the anther (the male part) to the stigma (the female part). It sounds small, but nothing can happen without it. If pollen never reaches a stigma, no seeds will form, no fruit will grow, and the plant cannot reproduce. So the whole future of the plant depends on this journey of a dusty little grain.

But here is the puzzle: a flower cannot walk, and pollen cannot fly on its own. So how does the pollen travel from one flower to another? Plants cannot move, so they hire helpers. The two most important helpers in your part of the world are animals (especially insects) and the wind. Let us look closely at each one, because plants have designed their flowers very cleverly to suit the helper they depend on.

Insect Pollination: Working With Bees and Butterflies

Picture a warm morning when a mango tree bursts into bloom. Soon the tree is buzzing with bees and fluttering with butterflies. These insects did not come to help the tree on purpose; they came because they are hungry. Flowers offer them a sweet reward called nectar, and bees also collect pollen as food. As an insect pushes into the flower to drink nectar, its furry body brushes against the anthers, and pollen sticks all over it, on its legs, its back, and its belly.

Then the insect flies to the next mango flower for another drink. This time, as it pushes in, some of the pollen already stuck to its body rubs off onto the sticky stigma of the new flower. Without even knowing it, the bee has carried pollen from one flower to another and completed pollination. The bee gets a meal, and the tree gets its pollen delivered. Both partners win, which is why scientists call this a mutually helpful relationship. A bee visiting hundreds of acacia or mango flowers in one day can pollinate a great many of them.

Because insect-pollinated flowers need to attract these helpers, they usually have big, bright, colourful petals, a sweet scent, and plenty of nectar. Some even have special patterns called nectar guides, like arrows painted on the petals, that point the insect toward the sugary reward. Everything about these flowers is designed to catch an insect's attention, much like a brightly painted shop tries to catch the eye of people walking past in a busy Eastleigh market.

Wind Pollination: Letting the Breeze Do the Work

Not every plant hires insects. Grasses, and crops such as maize, use a completely free helper: the wind. Instead of making bright petals and sweet nectar, which cost the plant a lot of energy, these plants make huge amounts of very light, dry pollen and simply release it into the moving air. The breeze catches the pollen and carries it, sometimes for long distances, until a few lucky grains happen to land on the stigma of another flower of the same kind.

This is why wind-pollinated flowers look so different from a hibiscus or a mango blossom. They are usually small, plain, and greenish or brown, with no bright colours, little or no scent, and no nectar, because they are not trying to attract any animal at all. Instead, their anthers often dangle outside the flower where the wind can reach them easily, and their stigmas are often large and feathery so they can comb pollen out of the passing air. If you gently shake the tassel at the top of a maize plant on a dry day, you will see a small cloud of pollen drift away on the breeze. That cloud is wind pollination happening right in front of you.

Did You Know? A single maize tassel can release more than two million grains of pollen! Wind-pollinated plants make so much pollen because most of it blows away and never lands on a stigma. Making millions of grains means at least a few will reach their target.
concepts.example: There is even a third, rarer helper. A few water plants let their pollen float on the surface of a pond or river until it reaches another flower. This is called water pollination, and while you will not see it as often, it shows just how many clever ways plants have found to solve the same problem of moving pollen from one flower to another.

concepts.title: From Pollination to Fertilisation to Fruit
concepts.explanation:
Pollination is only the delivery of the pollen. The real magic happens next, and it is called fertilisation. Once a pollen grain lands on the sticky stigma, it does something remarkable: it grows a tiny tube. This pollen tube pushes its way down through the style and into the ovary. Inside the pollen tube travels a male cell. When that male cell reaches an ovule and joins with the egg cell inside it, fertilisation is complete. That joining is the exact moment a seed begins to form. Think of pollination as posting a letter and fertilisation as the letter finally being opened and read.

It is important to understand that pollination and fertilisation are not the same thing. Pollination is the journey of the pollen to the stigma. Fertilisation is the joining of the male cell with the ovule deep inside the ovary. Pollination must happen first, and fertilisation follows only if the pollen reaches the right place. Many students mix these two words up, so say them out loud a few times and picture what each one means.

After fertilisation, the flower begins to change in a wonderful way. The bright petals have done their job of attracting pollinators, so they wilt, dry up, and fall off, and the plant no longer wastes energy on them. Meanwhile, the ovary starts to swell and grow. Slowly, over days and weeks, that ovary ripens into a fruit, and the ovules inside it become seeds. This is the step that puts food on your table.

Here is the part that surprises many people: a mango is a swollen, ripened ovary. So is a papaya, a banana, a tomato, and a guava. Every juicy fruit you enjoy was once the ovary at the base of a flower. When Amina bites into a sweet mango in Kismaayo, she is really eating the grown-up ovary of a mango flower that a bee helped to pollinate weeks earlier. The seeds hidden inside a fruit are the grown-up ovules. Understanding this changes the way you look at every meal.

Did You Know? The reason a mango or a papaya is sweet, soft and brightly coloured is not for us at all. It is a trick to make animals want to eat it, so that the animal will carry the seeds inside to a new place. The plant is paying the animal with sweetness in exchange for a ride for its seeds.
concepts.example: Not all fruits are soft and juicy. Some are dry and hard. The long pods that hang from an acacia tree are fruits too, even though they are dry and woody. Inside those pods are the acacia seeds. A peanut shell, a bean pod, and the woody fruit of a baobab are all dry fruits. Whether a fruit is soft like a banana or dry like an acacia pod, it has the same two jobs: to protect the seeds while they grow, and to help spread them to new places. That second job is so important that it gets a whole part of this unit to itself.

concepts.title: Seed Dispersal, How Plants Travel Without Legs
concepts.explanation:
Imagine a baobab tree drops all its seeds straight down and every single seed sprouts right below the parent. Very quickly there would be dozens of tiny baobabs crowded together in the shade of the big tree, all fighting for the same water, the same sunlight, and the same patch of soil. Most of them would not survive. This is the problem every plant must solve, and the solution is called seed dispersal: spreading seeds away from the parent so they can find their own space to grow.

Ask yourself the key question: why don't plants want their seeds to grow right next to them? The answer is competition. Seeds that land far from the parent plant find fresh soil, their own sunlight, and their own water, and they are far more likely to survive and grow into healthy adult plants. Dispersal also lets plants spread into new areas, so a single acacia can, over many years, help fill a whole stretch of savanna with acacia trees. Because plants cannot walk, they have invented several brilliant ways to send their seeds on a journey. Let us meet each one.

Some seeds are built to fly. They are very light and often have wings, hairs, or little parachutes that catch the air. When the breeze blows, these seeds are lifted up and carried far away from the parent plant. The fluffy seeds of many savanna grasses drift across the plains this way, and the seed heads of certain trees spin like tiny helicopters as they fall. On the dry, windy plains of the Rift Valley, wind is one of the most powerful seed-carriers of all.

Animals move seeds in two very different ways. The first way is on the outside of their bodies. Some seeds have tiny hooks or sticky surfaces that catch onto the fur of a goat, a camel, or a donkey, or onto your own clothes as you walk through the bush. The animal carries these hitchhiking seeds far away and they eventually drop off in a new place. The second way is on the inside. When an elephant, a monkey, a baboon or a bird eats a sweet fruit like a wild fig or a berry, it swallows the seeds too. The seeds pass safely through the animal's body and come out later, often many kilometres away, dropped in a pile of natural fertiliser. Elephants are famous for spreading the seeds of large fruits across huge distances in this way, and birds carry small seeds from tree to tree all day long.

Did You Know? Some seeds actually grow better after passing through an animal's stomach. The animal's digestive juices soften the tough seed coat, which helps the seed sprout more easily once it lands in the soil. The animal gets a meal and the seed gets both a ride and a helping hand!

Plants that grow near rivers, lakes, or the Indian Ocean coast can use water to move their seeds. These seeds are light and waterproof so they can float. A coconut is the champion of water dispersal: it can float on the ocean for a very long time and travel to a distant beach before sprouting. Along the Jubba River, floodwaters carry many kinds of seeds downstream to fresh mud where they can grow.

A few clever plants do not wait for wind, water, or animals at all. They fling their own seeds away. As their dry pods ripen in the hot sun, tension builds up inside until, suddenly, the pod snaps open with a pop and shoots the seeds out in every direction. Many bean and pea family plants do exactly this. If you have ever heard a faint crackling from dry pods on a hot afternoon, you may have been listening to explosive seed dispersal.
concepts.example: Notice how the shape of a seed gives away its travel plan. A light, feathery seed is built for the wind. A hooked, prickly seed is built to grab a passing animal. A juicy fruit around a seed is an invitation for an animal to eat and carry it. A floating, waterproof seed is built for a river or the sea. When you find any seed, you can look at its shape and make a good scientist's guess about how it travels. That is exactly the kind of thinking a real botanist does.

concepts.title: The Full Circle, the Life Cycle of a Flowering Plant
concepts.explanation:
Now let us put all the pieces together into one big story that never ends. This story is called the life cycle of a flowering plant, and it moves in a circle. Follow it step by step and you will see how everything you have learned fits together.

A seed rests in the soil. When it has enough water and warmth, it sprouts. The tiny root pushes down and the tiny shoot pushes up. This is germination.

A seedling grows. It develops leaves and uses sunlight, water, and air to make its own food, becoming bigger and stronger every day.

A mature plant forms. When it is old enough, the plant grows flowers, the special structures built for reproduction.

Pollination happens. A bee, a butterfly, or the wind carries pollen from an anther to a stigma.

Fertilisation follows. A pollen tube grows down to an ovule, the male cell joins the egg cell, and a seed begins to form.

Fruit and seeds develop. The petals fall, the ovary swells into a fruit, and the ovules become seeds inside it.

Dispersal spreads the seeds. Wind, water, animals, or an exploding pod carries the seeds to new ground, and the whole circle begins again from step one.

This circle has been turning for longer than anyone can imagine. Every mango tree, every stalk of maize, and every acacia on the savanna is one link in a chain that stretches back through countless generations of plants. When Yusuf plants a mango seed today, he is joining that ancient circle and helping it continue for the people who come after him. Understanding the life cycle is understanding how life keeps renewing itself.
concepts.example: The timing of this circle is guided by the seasons, and that is why farmers watch the sky so carefully. In many parts of East Africa the rains come at certain times of the year, and plants have learned to flower and fruit so that their seeds land in moist soil ready to sprout. A mango tree often flowers in the dry season so that its fruit is ripe by the time the rains arrive. Grasses on the savanna burst into flower and scatter their seeds just before the wet season, so that the young plants have water to grow. When you notice which month the flowers appear, which month the fruit ripens, and which month the seeds are spread, you are reading the calendar that plants have followed for thousands of years, and you are thinking exactly like a farmer and a scientist at the same time.

concepts.title: Reading Corner: The Mango Tree in Halima's Garden
concepts.explanation:
Read this short passage carefully, then answer the questions that follow. Take your time, and look back at the passage whenever you need to.

In the corner of Halima's family compound near Kismaayo grows a tall mango tree that her grandfather planted long ago. One morning in the dry season, Halima noticed that the tree was covered in hundreds of small, pale flowers, and the air around it was buzzing loudly. When she looked closely, she saw bees crawling over the blossoms and a butterfly resting on one flower with its long tongue reaching in for nectar. "They are drinking the sweet juice," her mother explained, "and while they drink, they are carrying yellow pollen from flower to flower. That is how the tree will make mangoes." Weeks later, Halima saw that the petals had dropped and small green lumps were growing where some of the flowers had been. Her mother told her these were baby mangoes, growing from the part of the flower called the ovary. All through the wet season the green mangoes swelled and ripened, until at last they turned golden and sweet. Halima picked one, and as she ate it she found the large seed in the middle. "If we plant this seed," her mother said, "one day it may grow into a mango tree as tall as this one, God willing."

explorations.title: Take a Flower Apart
explorations.context: To find and name the parts of a real flower by carefully taking one apart. Make a Prediction: Before you start, write down: How many petals do you think your flower has? Will you be able to find the sticky stigma and the dusty anthers? Write your guesses so you can check them later. What You Need (Household Only) One large fresh flower you are allowed to pick, such as a hibiscus, a lily, or any big garden flower. A sheet of paper or a plate to lay the parts on. A magnifying glass if you have one (not essential). Sticky tape and a pencil for labelling. What To Do: Look at the whole flower first. Notice its colour and smell. Does it look built to attract insects? Gently pull off the green sepals at the base and lay them on the left of your paper. Next remove the petals one by one. Count them and lay them beside the sepals. Find the stamens (the stalks with dusty tips). Rub an anther on the paper; the powder is pollen. Find the pistil in the centre. Touch the top gently; the sticky part is the stigma. If an adult helps you, carefully split open the ovary at the base of the pistil. Look for tiny ovules inside; these would have become seeds. Tape each part onto paper and label it: sepal, petal, stamen, anther, pistil, stigma, ovary. Record Your Observations: What I Observed: My Result: Number of sepals Number of petals Colour of petals Pollen colour Was the stigma sticky? (yes/no) Ovules found inside ovary? (yes/no) Think About It: Which parts were the male parts and which were the female parts? Was the stigma sticky? Why is that useful during pollination? From its colour and smell, do you think insects or the wind pollinate this flower?
explorations.prompt: What do you predict will happen in Take a Flower Apart?
explorations.answer: Carry out take a flower apart, record exactly what you observe, and compare it with the prediction you wrote before you started.

explorations.title: Make a Spinning Seed and Test Wind Dispersal
explorations.context: To find out how the shape of a wind-dispersed seed helps it stay in the air longer and travel further. Make a Prediction: Do you think a seed with wide wings will fall slower or faster than a seed with small wings? Write your prediction before you test. What You Need (Household Only) A sheet of paper. A pair of scissors (use with an adult nearby). A small paper clip or a tiny piece of sticky tape for weight. A ruler. What To Do: Cut a strip of paper about 3 cm wide and 15 cm long to be your model seed with wings. Fold the bottom up and add a paper clip so it has a little weight, like a real seed. Cut two 'wings' at the top and fold one wing forward and one backward, like a letter Y from above. Stand on a safe step (with an adult) and drop your paper seed. Watch it spin as it falls. Now cut the wings much smaller and drop it again from the same height. Drop each version three times and count slowly to see how long each stays in the air. Record Your Observations: Test Result Big wings, drop 1 / 2 / 3 (count) Small wings, drop 1 / 2 / 3 (count) Which spun more? Which stayed up longer? Think About It: Which model seed stayed in the air longer, big wings or small wings? Why would staying in the air longer help a real seed travel further from its parent plant? How is your paper model like the fluffy grass seeds that blow across the savanna?

explorations.title: Sort Seeds by How They Travel
explorations.context: To collect different seeds from around your home and work out how each one is dispersed by looking at its shape. Make a Prediction Which do you think you will find more of: seeds built to fly on the wind, or seeds built to be eaten by animals? Write your guess. What You Need (Household Only) Seeds you can safely find at home: bean seeds, maize kernels, mango or papaya seeds, tomato seeds, seeds stuck to your socks after a walk, fluffy seeds from grasses or weeds. A plate or tray and some paper. A magnifying glass if you have one. What To Do Collect as many different seeds as you safely can. Ask an adult which ones are safe to handle. Lay them on your tray and look closely at each one. For each seed, ask: Is it light and fluffy? Does it have hooks? Did it come from a juicy fruit? Is it light enough to float? Sort the seeds into four groups: wind, animal (hooks), animal (eaten in fruit), and water. Draw each seed and write which group you put it in and why. Record Your Observations Dispersal Group Seeds I Placed Here Wind (light / fluffy / winged) Animal — hooks or sticky Animal — inside a juicy fruit Water — light and floats Think About It Which group had the most seeds? Why might that be, where you live? Take one seed and explain exactly how its shape matches its way of travelling. Try floating one seed in a cup of water. Does it float or sink? What does that tell you?

explorations.title: Be the Bee - Hand Pollination
explorations.context: To act like a pollinator by moving pollen from one flower to another, and to understand exactly what a bee does. Make a Prediction: Do you think you can move visible pollen from one flower to another using a cotton bud? What colour will the pollen be? Write your prediction. What You Need (Household Only) Two fresh flowers of the same kind that have visible pollen (a hibiscus or a pumpkin flower works well). A cotton bud, a small clean paintbrush, or even a soft feather. White paper to see the pollen clearly. What To Do: Gently brush the cotton bud against the anthers of the first flower. Look; pollen should stick to it. Tap the cotton bud on white paper so you can see the pollen grains you collected. Now brush that same pollen gently onto the sticky stigma in the centre of the second flower. You have just done by hand exactly what a bee does by accident! Wash your hands afterward. If the flower is on a living plant you may watch over the next weeks to see if a small fruit begins to grow where you pollinated it. Record Your Observations: Observation Result Colour of the pollen Did pollen stick to the cotton bud? (yes/no) Did pollen transfer to the stigma? (yes/no) If watching a plant: did a fruit start to grow? Think About It: How is the cotton bud like the furry body of a bee? Why does the pollen stick to the cotton bud and then to the stigma so easily? Farmers sometimes hand-pollinate crops when there are too few bees. Why might that be necessary?

methods.title: Take a Flower Apart
methods.example: To find and name the parts of a real flower by carefully taking one apart. Make a Prediction: Before you start, write down: How many petals do you think your flower has? Will you be able to find the sticky stigma and the dusty anthers? Write your guesses so you can check them later. What You Need (Household Only) One large fresh flower you are allowed to pick, such as a hibiscus, a lily, or any big garden flower. A sheet of paper or a plate to lay the parts on. A magnifying glass if you have one (not essential). Sticky tape and a pencil for labelling. What To Do: Look at the whole flower first. Notice its colour and smell. Does it look built to attract insects? Gently pull off the green sepals at the base and lay them on the left of your paper. Next remove the petals one by one. Count them and lay them beside the sepals. Find the stamens (the stalks with dusty tips). Rub an anther on the paper; the powder is pollen. Find the pistil in the centre. Touch the top gently; the sticky part is the stigma. If an adult helps you, carefully split open the ovary at the base of the pistil. Look for tiny ovules inside; these would have become seeds. Tape each part onto paper and label it: sepal, petal, stamen, anther, pistil, stigma, ovary. Record Your Observations: What I Observed: My Result: Number of sepals Number of petals Colour of petals Pollen colour Was the stigma sticky? (yes/no) Ovules found inside ovary? (yes/no) Think About It: Which parts were the male parts and which were the female parts? Was the stigma sticky? Why is that useful during pollination? From its colour and smell, do you think insects or the wind pollinate this flower?
steps: Observe carefully and record what you see.
Compare your result with your hypothesis.

methods.title: Make a Spinning Seed and Test Wind Dispersal
methods.example: To find out how the shape of a wind-dispersed seed helps it stay in the air longer and travel further. Make a Prediction: Do you think a seed with wide wings will fall slower or faster than a seed with small wings? Write your prediction before you test. What You Need (Household Only) A sheet of paper. A pair of scissors (use with an adult nearby). A small paper clip or a tiny piece of sticky tape for weight. A ruler. What To Do: Cut a strip of paper about 3 cm wide and 15 cm long to be your model seed with wings. Fold the bottom up and add a paper clip so it has a little weight, like a real seed. Cut two 'wings' at the top and fold one wing forward and one backward, like a letter Y from above. Stand on a safe step (with an adult) and drop your paper seed. Watch it spin as it falls. Now cut the wings much smaller and drop it again from the same height. Drop each version three times and count slowly to see how long each stays in the air. Record Your Observations: Test Result Big wings, drop 1 / 2 / 3 (count) Small wings, drop 1 / 2 / 3 (count) Which spun more? Which stayed up longer? Think About It: Which model seed stayed in the air longer, big wings or small wings? Why would staying in the air longer help a real seed travel further from its parent plant? How is your paper model like the fluffy grass seeds that blow across the savanna?
steps: Observe carefully and record what you see.
Compare your result with your hypothesis.

methods.title: Sort Seeds by How They Travel
methods.example: To collect different seeds from around your home and work out how each one is dispersed by looking at its shape. Make a Prediction Which do you think you will find more of: seeds built to fly on the wind, or seeds built to be eaten by animals? Write your guess. What You Need (Household Only) Seeds you can safely find at home: bean seeds, maize kernels, mango or papaya seeds, tomato seeds, seeds stuck to your socks after a walk, fluffy seeds from grasses or weeds. A plate or tray and some paper. A magnifying glass if you have one. What To Do Collect as many different seeds as you safely can. Ask an adult which ones are safe to handle. Lay them on your tray and look closely at each one. For each seed, ask: Is it light and fluffy? Does it have hooks? Did it come from a juicy fruit? Is it light enough to float? Sort the seeds into four groups: wind, animal (hooks), animal (eaten in fruit), and water. Draw each seed and write which group you put it in and why. Record Your Observations Dispersal Group Seeds I Placed Here Wind (light / fluffy / winged) Animal — hooks or sticky Animal — inside a juicy fruit Water — light and floats Think About It Which group had the most seeds? Why might that be, where you live? Take one seed and explain exactly how its shape matches its way of travelling. Try floating one seed in a cup of water. Does it float or sink? What does that tell you?
steps: Observe carefully and record what you see.
Compare your result with your hypothesis.

methods.title: Be the Bee - Hand Pollination
methods.example: To act like a pollinator by moving pollen from one flower to another, and to understand exactly what a bee does. Make a Prediction: Do you think you can move visible pollen from one flower to another using a cotton bud? What colour will the pollen be? Write your prediction. What You Need (Household Only) Two fresh flowers of the same kind that have visible pollen (a hibiscus or a pumpkin flower works well). A cotton bud, a small clean paintbrush, or even a soft feather. White paper to see the pollen clearly. What To Do: Gently brush the cotton bud against the anthers of the first flower. Look; pollen should stick to it. Tap the cotton bud on white paper so you can see the pollen grains you collected. Now brush that same pollen gently onto the sticky stigma in the centre of the second flower. You have just done by hand exactly what a bee does by accident! Wash your hands afterward. If the flower is on a living plant you may watch over the next weeks to see if a small fruit begins to grow where you pollinated it. Record Your Observations: Observation Result Colour of the pollen Did pollen stick to the cotton bud? (yes/no) Did pollen transfer to the stigma? (yes/no) If watching a plant: did a fruit start to grow? Think About It: How is the cotton bud like the furry body of a bee? Why does the pollen stick to the cotton bud and then to the stigma so easily? Farmers sometimes hand-pollinate crops when there are too few bees. Why might that be necessary?

workedExamples.title: Guided example 1
workedExamples.prompt: Which part of a flower produces pollen? (a) pistil (b) petals (c) anther (d) sepal
workedExamples.solution: c) anther. The anther is the pollen-making tip of the stamen.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: The main job of colourful petals is to: (a) protect the bud (b) attract pollinators (c) make seeds (d) store water
workedExamples.solution: b) attract pollinators. Bright petals advertise the flower to bees, butterflies and birds.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: Which part of the flower grows into a fruit after fertilisation? (a) stamen (b) petal (c) ovary (d) sepal
workedExamples.solution: c) ovary. After fertilisation the ovary swells and ripens into the fruit.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: The sticky top of the pistil that catches pollen is the: (a) style (b) ovary (c) stigma (d) anther
workedExamples.solution: c) stigma. The stigma is sticky so it can catch pollen grains.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Sepals mainly: (a) attract insects (b) make nectar (c) protect the flower bud (d) release pollen
workedExamples.solution: c) protect the flower bud. Sepals wrap around and guard the bud before it opens.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: Moving pollen from an anther to a stigma is called: (a) fertilisation (b) germination (c) pollination (d) dispersal
workedExamples.solution: c) pollination. Pollination is the movement of pollen to the stigma.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: Which flower is most likely pollinated by the wind? (a) a bright hibiscus (b) a plain green grass flower (c) a scented rose (d) a red tubular flower
workedExamples.solution: b) a plain green grass flower. Wind-pollinated flowers are small and dull, not colourful.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: A juicy mango is really the plant's swollen: (a) ovary (b) petal (c) stamen (d) sepal
workedExamples.solution: a) ovary. A mango is the ripened, swollen ovary of a mango flower.

rules.title: From Flower to Seed to New Plant
rules.text: A flower makes seeds. Pollination moves the pollen; fertilisation starts the seed; the ovary becomes the fruit; and dispersal carries the seeds to new ground so the life cycle can begin all over again.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the three parts that make up the pistil.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The pistil is made of the stigma, the style, and the ovary.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between pollination and fertilisation.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Pollination is moving pollen from the anther to the stigma. Fertilisation happens afterward, when the male cell from the pollen joins an ovule inside the ovary to start a seed. Pollination comes first; fertilisation follows.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why are insect-pollinated flowers usually brightly coloured and scented?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Bright colour and sweet scent attract insect pollinators such as bees and butterflies, which the flower needs to carry its pollen. The petals act like an advertisement.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What happens to the petals of a flower after it has been fertilised?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The petals wilt and fall off because they have finished their job of attracting pollinators, and the plant no longer needs to spend energy on them.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Describe two different ways that animals disperse seeds.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Any two: (1) Seeds with hooks or sticky surfaces catch on animal fur and are carried away; (2) Seeds inside juicy fruits are eaten and later passed out in the animal's droppings far away.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is it bad for a plant if all its seeds land right beneath it?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: If all seeds land beneath the parent, they must compete for the same water, light and soil, so most will not survive. Spreading out helps more of them live.

selfAssessment: I can name and describe the main parts of a flower and explain the job each part does.
I can explain pollination and describe how insects such as bees and butterflies, and how the wind, carry pollen from one flower to another.
I can describe fertilisation and explain how a flower changes into a fruit after it has been pollinated.
I can explain how seeds form inside a fruit and why each seed can grow into a brand-new plant.
I can compare the flowers of insect-pollinated plants (like mango) with wind-pollinated plants (like maize).
I can describe several ways seeds are dispersed by wind, by water, by animals, and by exploding pods, and explain why spreading out helps plants survive.
I can put the whole life cycle in order, from seed to seedling to flowering plant to fruit and back to seed.
I can investigate flowers and seeds safely at home and record what you observe like a real scientist.
